Scientists Discover Breakthrough in Carbon Capture Technology

By Jane Smith · 12 May 2026

Researchers at the University of Cambridge have announced a major breakthrough in carbon capture technology that could significantly accelerate efforts to combat climate change. The new method uses a novel chemical process to extract carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at a fraction of the cost of existing solutions.

The team spent over five years developing the technique, which relies on specially engineered enzymes derived from deep-sea bacteria. Unlike current carbon capture systems, which require enormous amounts of energy to operate, this new approach operates at ambient temperature and pressure.

"This is a genuine paradigm shift," said Professor Alan Davies, the lead researcher on the project. "We have shown that it is possible to capture carbon at scale without the prohibitive energy costs that have made previous attempts economically unviable."

The discovery has attracted attention from governments and corporations around the world. Several major energy companies have already expressed interest in licensing the technology, and the research team is in discussions with the European Union about a pilot programme to begin testing the approach on an industrial scale.

Critics have noted that scaling the technology will present its own challenges. Supply chains for the required enzyme precursors are currently limited, and there are open questions about long-term storage of the captured carbon. Nevertheless, independent experts have broadly welcomed the announcement as a significant step forward.

The findings were published today in the journal Nature Energy and have already been cited as a potential game-changer by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
